question: An environmental impact assessment1 is being carried out for a private marina and cruise port in Fiumicino (Rome) which the Italian Government has included2 among the Catholic Church’s Jubilee projects. It will not be completed in time3, but it is still benefiting from expedited authorisation procedures.

The port is part of a state-owned maritime concession4 that runs until 2100 and was obtained in 2010 by IP Iniziative Portuale for a simple marina. Owing to financial troubles, the concession was put up for sale after authorities amended it in 2018 to include cruise activity. Fiumicino Waterfront bought it.

Now that cruise activity is included, the port’s infrastructure and activities are enough to suggest that – if they are even appropriate at all – the concession in question should have been awarded by means of a special European tender.

According to press reports5, the cost of the port exceeds EUR 500 million, which alone is practically the same as the turnover that a concession must accrue over time to fall within the scope of Directive 2014/23/EU. That directive provides only for an agreement already in force to be amended in limited cases and without altering its general nature. In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission investigate the matter further with a view to checking whether Directive 2014/23/EU is being upheld?
If Directive 2014/23/EU has not been upheld, what measures will it take?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.3.2025) Directive 2014/23/EU1 applies to the award of concession contracts within the meaning of Article 5(1) of that Directive with a value exceeding the thresholds laid down in that same Directive.

Under Article 43 of Directive 2014/23/EU, concessions may be modified during their term without a new procurement procedure only provided that the conditions laid down exhaustively in the first two paragraphs of that provision are met.

In the case at hand, based on the elements available, it is unclear whether the contract referred to in the Honourable Members’ question can be qualified as a concession within the meaning of Directive 2014/23/EU or whether it should rather be considered as an authorisation for the pursuit of an economic activity falling outside the scope of that Directive.

However, should the contract referred to by the Honourable Members fall within the scope of Directive 2014/23/EU, the national review bodies laid down under the Directives on remedies in public procurement (Directive 89/665/EEC2 and Directive 92/13/EEC3, as amended by Directive 2007/66/EC4 and Directive 2014/23/EU) are in the best position to assess, according to the facts of each case, whether these requirements are met in the specific dispute, and therefore whether contracting authorities and contracting entities respected their obligations under EU law.
